analysis.one_liner: Lets states fold all residents into one publicly run, comprehensive health plan funded by existing federal health dollars.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: referred to five House committees in November 2023, it sat in a subcommittee until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let a state, or a group of states, apply to set up its own universal health care program covering all residents, run by a public agency. The state would waive a long list of federal health rules — including parts of the Affordable Care Act, Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, federal employee and military coverage, ACA tax credits, and the employer insurance rules — and instead receive the money the federal government would have spent on those programs in that state. The state plan would have to be at least as comprehensive and affordable as the programs it replaces, cover 95% of residents within five years, and be publicly administered, with an independent panel reviewing each state's application.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of any state that adopts it: everyone would get comprehensive coverage regardless of job, income, or health status, including lawfully residing immigrants. American Indians and Alaska Natives would have all costs covered by the federal government with no premiums or copays, and Indian health providers would get paid for services to enrollees.

how_it_helps.text: A state plan must cover all residents and be at least as comprehensive and as affordable as the federal programs it replaces, with protections against excessive out-of-pocket costs.

The state receives the aggregate federal money that would otherwise have been spent in the state on Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA subsidies and tax credits, federal employee and military health coverage, adjusted for caseload growth and medical inflation, and may reinvest any savings in health services.
Coverage must include reproductive health care including abortion, contraception, and gender-affirming care, and must keep accessible complaints, appeals, and independent review procedures.

American Indians and Alaska Natives enrolled through a state plan pay no premiums, deductibles, or copays; the federal government bears those costs, and insurers must contract with and pay Indian health care providers.

Applications get public notice and comment, an independent assessment panel review, annual public reporting on how waiver funds were spent, and an independent five-year review with public hearings; a state that fails to reach 95% coverage gets technical assistance and a 12-month grace period, and can lose the waiver.

analysis.who_pays: States adopting it must produce a 10-year budget plan that is budget-neutral for the federal government, meaning state revenue would have to cover costs beyond the federal passthrough. Private insurers would lose the comprehensive coverage market in a participating state, and employers would no longer be bound by the federal employer mandate or ERISA rules within the state, with financing shifted to the state plan.

drawbacks.text: Because the federal money is capped at an aggregate amount (with caseload growth and inflation adjustments), a state whose health costs rise faster would have to make up the difference from its own revenue, likely through new state taxes.

Transitions are risky: a state must reach 95% coverage within five years or, after a grace period, the Secretary may terminate the waiver, which could leave residents back in the old fragmented system mid-transition.

The waiver list includes employer coverage rules (the ACA employer mandate and ERISA), so a participating state's workers with job-based plans would move into the state plan, a large administrative and political transition, though the state may contract with private entities to help administer the plan.

The bill leaves the actual financing method entirely to each state, and no state has a ready plan, so the practical path from waiver to coverage would depend on each state passing new funding legislation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design has real protections: coverage floors at least as strong as the programs replaced, public administration, public comment and independent five-year reviews, and special safeguards for Native Americans. The serious cost is that each participating state must finance whatever the capped federal passthrough does not cover, and the transition could be disruptive. It was an option states could decline, not a mandate. On the merits it is a substantial potential gain for the uninsured and underinsured in participating states, weighed against significant state fiscal and transition risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees the day it was introduced, sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on November 7, 2023, joined by 27 original cosponsors, all Democrats.

The Speaker's referral split the bill among five committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, Oversight, and Education and the Workforce — a routing that requires each committee with jurisdiction to act before the bill can advance.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on November 10, 2023, and re-referred there on December 17, 2024; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote at any point.
The bill ended the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 with 30 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no recorded action beyond subcommittee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers keep the comprehensive coverage market intact, since no state gained the authority to replace private coverage with a public plan. The 31 sponsoring and cosponsoring members gained nothing, and residents of states that might have applied saw no change. Because the bill required state legislation to activate, its death had no immediate practical effect on anyone's coverage.

for.name: Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the State-Based Universal Health Care Act on November 7, 2023.

for.name: 30 House cosponsors
for.role: Original and additional cosponsors, all Democrats (including Jayapal, Pocan, Pressley, Tlaib, McGovern, Schakowsky)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; none chaired a committee with jurisdiction over the bill.

against.name: House committee chairs (Energy and Commerce; Ways and Means)
against.role: Chairs of the two committees with primary jurisdiction over health coverage and federal health financing, Republican majority in the 118th House
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the record shows no committee action after the Health Subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority party of the 118th House
against.what_they_did: Routed the bill to five committees for piecemeal consideration and never brought it to the floor during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it; the Republican-held House took no action on the bill at any point in the Congress.

industries.note: A state plan must be publicly administered and would fold Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA marketplace coverage, and federal-employee and military coverage into one program, with public education about restrictions on duplicative private coverage — sharply shrinking the market for comprehensive private insurance in any participating state. States may still contract with private entities to administer the plan. The bill's death preserves the existing private market.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug makers and other health price-setters
industries.note: A single publicly administered plan covering nearly all residents of a state would give that state the bargaining position of one large purchaser for drugs and services, the mechanism by which single-payer systems obtain lower prices. No state obtained that authority.

industries.industry: Employers that currently provide health coverage
industries.note: In a participating state the federal employer mandate and ERISA self-insured plan rules would be waived, freeing employers from coverage obligations, but the state would presumably need new revenue to finance the plan. The bill died, so no employer's obligations changed.

Guaranteed coverage for all residents would sharply cut uncompensated care, but a consolidated public payer would likely pay lower rates than private insurers. Providers in non-participating states, which is all of them, see no change.

industries.industry: Indian health care providers and tribal health programs
industries.note: The federal government must cover all costs for American Indian and Alaska Native enrollees, with no cost sharing, and insurers must contract with and pay Indian health providers at no less than participating-provider rates — a direct funding gain, though no state program was ever established.
